{{short description|Type of curve in geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''prime geodesic''' on a [[hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic]] [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] is a '''primitive''' [[closed geodesic]]: one whose parametrization is not obtained by going repeatedly around a shorter closed geodesic.<ref name="Buser1992">{{cite book |last=Buser |first=Peter |title=Geometry and Spectra of Compact Riemann Surfaces |publisher=Birkhäuser |location=Boston |year=1992}}</ref><ref name="Katok1992">{{cite book |last=Katok |first=Svetlana |title=Fuchsian Groups |publisher=University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago |year=1992}}</ref> Informally, one follows the geodesic until its motion begins to repeat; the geodesic is prime if this first full return already completes the entire cycle, rather than repeating a shorter cycle several times. For comparison, a [[great circle]] on a sphere traversed once is analogous to a prime geodesic, whereas the same great circle traversed twice is not. Prime geodesics play, for hyperbolic surfaces, a role analogous to that of [[prime number]]s in [[number theory]]: every closed geodesic is obtained by iterating a prime geodesic, and their [[asymptotic distribution]] is described by the '''prime geodesic theorem'''.<ref name="Iwaniec1984">{{cite journal |last=Iwaniec |first=Henryk |title=Prime geodesic theorem |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik |volume=349 |year=1984 |pages=136–159 |doi=10.1515/crll.1984.349.136}}</ref>

==Definition==
Let <math>X</math> be a hyperbolic surface. A closed geodesic <math>\gamma</math> on <math>X</math> is called '''prime''' or '''primitive''' if it is not an iterate <math>\gamma_0^n</math> of another closed geodesic <math>\gamma_0</math> with <math>n \ge 2</math>.<ref name="Buser1992" /> Equivalently, a closed geodesic is prime if it traverses its image exactly once.

Every closed geodesic on a hyperbolic surface is an iterate of a unique prime geodesic.<ref name="Buser1992" /><ref name="Katok1992" />

Note: A geodesic is not considered closed merely because its image crosses itself. To be closed, it must return to its starting point with the same tangent direction; prime geodesics are those closed geodesics for which this first return is not itself a repetition of a shorter closed geodesic.

==Relation with Fuchsian groups==
If <math>X = \Gamma \backslash \mathbb{H}</math> is a hyperbolic surface presented as a quotient of the [[hyperbolic plane]] by a [[Fuchsian group]] <math>\Gamma \subset \mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{R})</math>, then each hyperbolic element of <math>\Gamma</math> has an invariant geodesic in <math>\mathbb{H}</math>, called its axis. The projection of this axis to <math>X</math> is a closed geodesic.<ref name="Katok1992" />

With the usual conventions, this gives a correspondence between closed geodesics on <math>X</math> and conjugacy classes of hyperbolic elements of <math>\Gamma</math>.<ref name="Katok1992" /><ref name="BorthwickSlides">{{cite web |last=Borthwick |first=David |title=Spectral Theory on Hyperbolic Surfaces |url=https://math.dartmouth.edu/~specgeom/Borthwick_slides.pdf |website=Dartmouth College |access-date=2026-04-02}}</ref> Under this correspondence, prime geodesics are exactly the conjugacy classes represented by ''primitive hyperbolic elements'', that is, elements that are not nontrivial powers of other elements of <math>\Gamma</math>.<ref name="Katok1992" />

If <math>P</math> is a prime geodesic of length <math>\ell(P)</math>, its ''norm'' is usually defined by
:<math>N(P)=e^{\ell(P)}.</math>
This normalization is standard in statements of the prime geodesic theorem and in the definition of the [[Selberg zeta function]].<ref name="Iwaniec1984" /><ref name="Terras2011">{{cite book |last=Terras |first=Audrey |title=Zeta Functions of Graphs: A Stroll through the Garden |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=2011 |chapter=Selberg zeta function}}</ref>

==Prime geodesic theorem==
Let
:<math>\pi_X(x)=\#\{P : P \text{ is a prime geodesic on } X,\ N(P)\le x\}.</math>

For a finite-area hyperbolic surface, the '''prime geodesic theorem''' states that
:<math>\pi_X(x)\sim \frac{x}{\log x}\qquad (x\to\infty).</math>
Equivalently, the number of prime geodesics of length at most <math>L</math> is asymptotic to <math>e^L/L</math> as <math>L\to\infty</math>.<ref name="Selberg1956">{{cite journal |last=Selberg |first=Atle |title=Harmonic analysis and discontinuous groups in weakly symmetric Riemannian spaces with applications to Dirichlet series |journal=Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society |series=New Series |volume=20 |year=1956 |pages=47–87}}</ref><ref name="Iwaniec1984" />

This theorem is an analogue of the [[prime number theorem]]. More refined versions include error terms, weighted counting functions analogous to the [[Chebyshev function]], and arithmetic refinements for special surfaces such as the [[modular curve|modular surface]].<ref name="Iwaniec1984" /><ref name="SoundYoung2013">{{cite journal |last1=Soundararajan |first1=Kannan |last2=Young |first2=Matthew P. |title=The prime geodesic theorem |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik |volume=676 |year=2013 |pages=105–120 |doi=10.1515/crelle.2012.002|arxiv=1011.5486 }}</ref>

==Selberg zeta function==
Prime geodesics enter the theory of hyperbolic surfaces through the [[Selberg zeta function]], an [[Euler product]] taken over prime geodesics:
:<math>Z_X(s)=\prod_{P}\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(1-N(P)^{-s-k}\right),</math>
where <math>P</math> ranges over the prime geodesics on <math>X</math>.<ref name="Terras2011" />

The analytic properties of <math>Z_X(s)</math> are closely related to spectral data of the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]] on the surface, and the prime geodesic theorem can be proved using this relationship together with the [[Selberg trace formula]].<ref name="Selberg1956" /><ref name="Iwaniec1984" />

==Generalizations==
The analogy between prime numbers and primitive closed orbits extends beyond constant-curvature surfaces. For geodesic flows on compact manifolds of negative curvature, asymptotic formulas for primitive closed geodesics were established by [[Grigory Margulis]], and later developed in the broader setting of hyperbolic dynamical systems.<ref name="Margulis2003">{{cite book |last=Margulis |first=Grigorii A. |title=On Some Aspects of the Theory of Anosov Systems: With a Survey by Richard Sharp |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin |year=2003}}</ref><ref name="ParryPollicott1990">{{cite book |last1=Parry |first1=William |last2=Pollicott |first2=Mark |title=Zeta Functions and the Periodic Orbit Structure of Hyperbolic Dynamics |series=Astérisque |volume=187–188 |publisher=Société Mathématique de France |year=1990}}</ref>

In a broader [[Riemannian geometry|Riemannian]] and [[dynamical systems]] context, the term ''prime geodesic'' is also used for a closed geodesic that is not an iterate of a shorter one, even when the surface is not hyperbolic.<ref name="AIM2010">{{cite web |title=Open problems and questions about geodesics |url=https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf |website=American Institute of Mathematics |year=2010 |access-date=2026-04-02}}</ref>
